summary: An IAB statement that the public DNS is a hierarchical name space derived from a single, globally unique root. It argues that the DNS cannot technically support more than one public root, which must be served by coordinated root servers under a unique naming authority. It is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: The Internet's public DNS depends on names having the same meaning for everyone. RFC 2826 argues that this requires one coordinated root, while allowing private networks to use their own name spaces.

subtitle: Why the IAB argues that public DNS names need one coordinated root.

tldr.problem: The public Internet depends on DNS names having one meaning everywhere. Multiple public roots could give the same name different records to users on different networks.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB's argument follows from DNS hierarchy, single-maintainer domains, coordinated record changes, and root-server addresses configured outside the DNS itself.
tldr.outcome: The memo concludes that the public DNS requires one globally unique root and coordinated root servers. It does not prohibit private networks from operating private name spaces.

facts.label: Public DNS roots in the IAB's conclusion

today: RFC 2826 is an Informational memo published in May 2000. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the memo records the IAB's argument for a unique root in the public DNS.

sections.title: The IAB's Main Claim
sections.content:
RFC 2826 is an Informational technical comment from the Internet Architecture Board (IAB), not a standard. It argues that the public DNS is a hierarchy built from one globally unique root, and that a second public root could cause users to receive different records for the same name.

The IAB concludes that the root must be served by coordinated root servers under one naming authority. Private networks may run private name spaces, but names intended to be globally unique must come from the public DNS hierarchy.
sections.plainLanguage: The IAB says public DNS names must have one meaning across the Internet. It concludes that the public DNS needs one root, while private networks may use private names.

sections.title: A Shared Meaning for DNS Names
sections.content:
Communication requires a shared set of symbols and an agreed meaning for each symbol. The memo applies this idea to public DNS: at any given time, a DNS name should refer to one set of records describing its addresses, resources and services.

Because DNS is hierarchical, each domain needs a single maintainer responsible for its subdomains and records. The memo treats this as a technical requirement of the DNS design, including for the root domain.
sections.plainLanguage: A DNS name works across the Internet only when systems agree on what it means. The memo says each part of the DNS hierarchy needs one maintainer to prevent conflicting records.

sections.title: Why Domain Updates Need Coordination
sections.content:
The DNS protocol assumes that each domain has one owner and that its records are updated as one coordinated set. A client has no DNS mechanism for discovering and choosing between conflicting definitions; it returns the first matching records it finds and assumes they are valid.

The memo considers whether separate authorities could share a domain under agreed rules. It argues that those rules would themselves create one coordinated naming system, rather than independent public roots.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS clients do not compare conflicting definitions from different owners. The memo argues that authorities must agree on update rules to preserve one shared meaning for each name.

sections.title: Why the Root Is Difficult to Change
sections.content:
The addresses of root name servers are supplied mainly through out-of-band configuration. Unlike ordinary DNS data, this information has no automatic timeout, and the memo says it may remain out of date at some sites for years.

A resolver with stale root-server addresses may not know which conflicting answer is valid or how to stop using a malicious or faulty server. For that reason, the memo says root-address changes are harder than other DNS delegation changes and recommends infrequent updates and close coordination. DNSSEC can help, but the root's signing key also depends on out-of-band configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: Resolvers learn root-server addresses from configuration outside normal DNS updates. If that information is stale, changing the root servers is difficult, so the memo recommends cautious, coordinated changes.

sections.title: Private Names and Other Lookup Needs
sections.content:
The memo allows private networks to run their own name spaces. If a private network uses a name defined for the global Internet, however, it needs that information from the global DNS hierarchy.

The IAB notes that DNS is not designed to help when a user has only a vague or ambiguous description. It expects directory systems to help identify the intended name, after which that unique DNS name can be resolved through DNS.
sections.plainLanguage: A private network may use private names. A directory may help someone identify a public DNS name, but the resulting name still uses the shared public DNS.
